title: Hybrid Search Done Right & Advanced Retrieval
description: Fix RAG retrieval failures using BM25, HNSW, Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), parent-child chunking, metadata filtering, and reranking in .NET.

data.text: Why Enterprise RAG Fails with Naive Vector Search

Most enterprise RAG prototypes fail not because the LLM cannot reason, but because naive retrieval fails to find the right information. Pure dense vector search (such as embeddings over small text chunks) struggles with exact product codes, acronyms, customer names, financial SKUs, and specific query terms. At the same time, traditional keyword search (BM25) fails when users ask questions using different vocabulary than the indexed documentation.

data.title: The Production Retrieval Golden Rule
data.text: Production-grade RAG requires a multi-stage retrieval architecture: Hybrid Search (BM25 keyword search + HNSW dense vector search) combined using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), followed by Cross-Encoder Reranking and Security ACL Trimming.

data.text: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists from different search algorithms without requiring normalized scores. The RRF score for document d is calculated as the sum of reciprocals of its position across all rank lists: RRF_Score(d) = sum(1 / (k + rank_i(d))), where k is a smoothing constant (typically 60).

data.text: A common dilemma in RAG is chunk size: small chunks (e.g., 128 tokens) yield accurate vector similarity because they avoid diluting the semantic signal, but lack surrounding context when fed to the LLM. Large chunks (e.g., 1000 tokens) provide context, but embeddings become vague and noisy.

Parent-child retrieval solves this: index small child chunks (sentence or paragraph level) with vector embeddings, but link each child chunk back to its larger parent section (or document). During retrieval, you match on child chunks, but swap in the parent chunk to feed the LLM prompt.

In enterprise knowledge bases, users should only retrieve documents they have authorization to view. Security trimming must occur at retrieval time inside the vector query filter, not as an afterthought after LLM generation.

data.title: Key Ingestion Pipeline Principles
items: Document Content Hashing: Compute SHA-256 hash of raw document bytes; skip ingestion if hash matches existing index entry.
Parent-Child Chunk Mapping: Split documents into parent sections (800-1200 tokens) and subdivide into child vector chunks (150-250 tokens) with cross-referencing IDs.
Idempotent Upserts: Always use unique, deterministic record keys (e.g., {DocId}_{ChunkIndex}) so failed ingestion jobs can be safely retried without duplicating vectors.
Tombstone Deletions: When a source document is updated or deleted, remove all previous child chunks using parent ID batch deletion.
Citations & Provenance: Store source document URI, page numbers, and author metadata on every chunk to generate verifiable citations in user answers.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Naive dense vector search fails on precise terms, product codes, and domain acronyms
Hybrid search combines BM25 keyword matching and HNSW dense vector search using Reciprocal Rank Fusion
Parent-child retrieval decouples small-chunk vector matching from broad-chunk LLM comprehension context
Enforce security trimming directly in the retrieval query filter using user tenant and security group ACLs
Apply cross-encoder reranking to the top candidate pool to prioritize context relevance before sending to the LLM
data.takeaway: Enterprise RAG succeeds or fails at retrieval. Implementing hybrid search with RRF, parent-child expansion, and retrieval-time ACL trimming is the gold standard for accurate knowledge assistants.
